strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing genuine gaps in video understanding: the need for native multi-turn tool invocation in long-form reasoning scenarios

Technically sound methodology with three well-designed components: Task-Decoupled Attention Masking effectively isolates attention patterns, Verifiable Trajectory-Guided Reward elegantly balances exploration and efficiency, and dynamic visual quota provides practical budget management

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 7 video understanding benchmarks with consistent improvements (72.1% on MLLVi, 47.6% on LVBench, 46.5% on VideoMMU) and rigorous ablation studies validating each component's contribution
Significant dataset contribution: Seeker-173K with 173K tool-invocation trajectories addresses data scarcity in multi-turn video reasoning, enabling future research
Strong reproducibility support with detailed implementation details (Tables 7-8), hyperparameters, prompt templates (Appendix F), and concrete examples throughout the paper
Honest and comprehensive limitation discussion identifying context window constraints, tool scalability issues, and failure modes like 'Fake Thinking' phenomena
High-quality presentation with effective visualizations (Figures 1-3) and well-organized structure combining main results with detailed appendices
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: individual components (attention masking, GRPO-based RL, visual quotas) are adaptations of existing techniques rather than fundamental innovations, lacking comparisons with alternative masking or reward strategies

Overstated 'long-form' video claims: evaluation limited to ~6-minute videos at 2 FPS with 768-frame maximum per benchmark; no evaluation on truly long-form content (full movies, hour-long videos), contradicting the main contribution premise

Incomplete computational analysis: training costs (GPU hours, memory requirements), inference overhead of the RL stage, and end-to-end time not thoroughly characterized; Table 11 shows only marginal inference speedup
Insufficient statistical rigor: no confidence intervals, significance tests, or variance analysis across runs; unclear whether reported performance differences are statistically meaningful

Dataset construction concerns: human annotation effort not quantified, potential biases from verification process not discussed, reliance on proprietary LLMs (Gemini 2.5 Pro) limits reproducibility, no separate ablation isolating dataset contribution

Framework limitations inadequately addressed: interaction depth fixed at 8 turns (arbitrary), tool support limited to VideoCrop with limited discussion of extending to other modalities, context window constraints fundamentally limiting complex reasoning chains

Failure mode analysis insufficient: Section H identifies turn-limit exceeding issues and Section I reveals 'Fake Thinking' where reasoning contradicts retrieved evidence, but solutions mentioned only vaguely without principled approaches

Limited evaluation scope: English-only benchmarks, cross-lingual and cross-domain generalization untested, no evaluation on diverse video types; human verification enforced through annotations but generalization to different domains unclear

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple benchmarks (MLVU, LLVBench, VideoMMU, Video-Holmes) with strong empirical results and detailed ablation studies validating each component's contribution
Well-motivated problem addressing the challenging task of multi-hop reasoning over long videos with clear observation that existing approaches fail at dependency tracking
Extensive reproducibility documentation with detailed implementation details, hyperparameters, dataset statistics, and training procedures in appendices
Honest discussion of limitations and failure modes, including identification of 'fake thinking' phenomenon and transparent acknowledgment of context window constraints
Systematic data synthesis pipeline with four-stage construction process (clue localization, validity verification, trajectory generation, consistency check)
Ablation studies (Tables 3-5) systematically validate individual component contributions with clear performance impact analysis
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: TDAM is straightforward attention masking, VTGR combines standard reward engineering techniques, and data synthesis follows established pipelines rather than introducing fundamental innovations

Severe contradiction between 'long video' claim and actual 8-turn context window limitation; no evidence approach scales beyond this or handles truly long-form videos despite acknowledging this as future work

Unresolved 'fake thinking' phenomenon (Section I) where model produces valid intermediate reasoning but arrives at logically inconsistent answers, suggesting pattern-matching rather than genuine reasoning without proposed solutions

Circular dataset construction: Seeker-173K is built using the paper's own data synthesis methodology that mirrors inference procedures; extent of human validation unclear with no reported inter-annotator agreement metrics
Improvements over baselines are often incremental and inconsistent across benchmarks; many baseline comparisons drawn from different papers' metrics complicating fair assessment
Entirely metric-based evaluation without human validation of reasoning correctness; no error analysis categorizing failure modes or validation that automated metrics reflect true reasoning capability
No ablation testing whether methods transfer to other MLLM backbones beyond Qwen2.5-VL; results may be model-specific and lack generalizability
Tool invocation framework has fundamental design issues: blind exploration handled via ad-hoc turn decay factor (Eq. 5) with discontinuous boundary conditions rather than principled search strategy

strengths: Well-motivated problem with clear identification of limitations in existing approaches for long-form video understanding
Comprehensive technical solution combining three complementary mechanisms (TDAM, VTGR, dynamic visual quota) that effectively address distinct challenges
Extensive experimental validation across 7+ benchmarks with detailed ablation studies demonstrating contribution of each component
Large-scale, high-quality dataset (Seeker-173K with 173k trajectories) constructed with rigorous multi-stage verification pipeline
Strong empirical results achieving state-of-the-art or competitive performance (72.1% on VideoMME, 47.6% on MLVU, 46.5% on Video-Holmes) with ~3× efficiency improvement
Honest discussion of limitations and failure modes (e.g., 'fake thinking' cases) enhancing credibility
Excellent presentation with clear visualizations (Figures 1-4) and thorough qualitative analysis with concrete examples
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: TDAM is conceptually straightforward (task-specific attention masking), VTGR combines standard trajectory rewards similar to existing work (Min-o3), core contribution is engineering-focused rather than introducing novel insights

Unclear attribution of gains: Seeker-173K dataset appears critical but paper doesn't isolate contributions of method vs. dataset; no experiments applying Video-o3's method to other datasets to assess generalization

Incremental empirical improvements: While strong, gains over baselines are often modest (4.8% on VideoMME, reasonable but not dramatic on others) and uneven across tasks (weak performance on Video-Holmes at 46.5%)

Scalability limitations not addressed: Context window limited to 8 turns restricts reasoning depth; framework tightly coupled to VideoCrop tool reducing generalization; 'fake thinking' failures indicate brittleness in reasoning consistency

Reproducibility challenges: Complex multi-stage training pipeline (SFT + RL), data synthesis relies on proprietary models (Gemini 2.5 Pro for trajectories), hyperparameter sensitivity not explored, computational requirements during training not discussed

Evaluation limitations: Statistical significance not reported, temporal grounding gains modest (0.5-1.4%), human evaluation of reasoning quality absent, failure analysis limited to specific 'fake thinking' cases
Inference efficiency still substantial at 10.2 seconds per video with multiple forward passes, unsuitable for real-time applications despite 3× improvement over baselines

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 8+ benchmarks with consistent improvements and thorough ablations of each component
Substantial dataset contribution (Seeker-173K with 173K trajectories) featuring rigorous 4-stage validation pipeline and stratified task diversity
Well-motivated problem formulation addressing clear limitations of prior approaches (decoupled methods lack joint optimization; single-turn misses sparse clues)
Technically sound methodology combining task-decoupled attention masking, trajectory-guided reward, and dynamic quota mechanism with clear intuitions
Excellent presentation quality with effective visualizations and comprehensive appendix including implementation details, ablations, qualitative analyses, and honest limitations
Practical efficiency gains: 32.9% speedup over decoupled methods while using fewer visual tokens, with cross-model generalization demonstrated
Honest treatment of limitations including identification of 'fake thinking' phenomenon, context window constraints, and clear discussion of failure modes
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: core components (DAPO, attention masking, reward shaping) are established techniques; primary contribution is engineering their combination rather than fundamental innovation

Design choices lack deep justification: 10% masking ratio tested on only three values with marginal differences; reward weights (b₀, wg, λ) lack sensitivity analysis or grid search; constant Cfree=0.5 not compared to alternatives
Modest empirical improvements despite consistency: typical gains are 1-4% (e.g., 72.1% vs 69.9% on MLVU); absolute performance on harder tasks remains low (46.5% on Video-Holmes)

Incomplete analysis of key mechanisms: TDAM shows only +1.1% on LVBench when applied; VTGR components show counterintuitive results (removing Turn Decay Factor sometimes increases tool-call rates); unclear which IoU/IoP/IoG metrics matter most

Fundamental failure mode insufficiently addressed: Figure 14 shows blind exploration problem when subtle clues are missed, but proposed solution (flexible clue exploration) is vague and deferred to future work

Data synthesis pipeline concerns: depends on proprietary Gemini 2.5 Pro (undermining 'native' claim and reproducibility); validation filter-to-final ratio not specified; self-collected YouTube data bias/diversity not discussed
'Fake thinking' problem not deeply solved: TDAM only applied during SFT but full context available at inference; solution appears ad-hoc; Figure 15 still shows counterexamples despite good reasoning

Limited experimental scope: fixed 16k token budget (no accuracy-efficiency frontier), baseline comparisons use reproductions rather than original evaluations, turn limit of 8 not validated against 10/12/16-turn variants

strengths: Well-motivated problem: Long-form video understanding with sparse critical evidence is practically important and timely
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 8 benchmarks with consistent improvements and detailed ablation studies
Efficiency gains: 32-46% speedup over decoupled methods (Table 6) with fewer input/output tokens
Honest discussion of limitations including identified 'fake thinking' problem and failure cases (Appendices H-J)
Generalization studies: Results on smaller models (Qwen3-VL-4B, Table 7) and free-format data scalability (Table 15) demonstrate broader applicability
weaknesses: Synthetic data circularity: Seeker-173K generated by more powerful model (Gemini 2.5 Pro). No ablation decomposing improvements from method vs. data quality. Table 14 shows SFT alone achieves most gains, suggesting data dominates.

Limited technical novelty: TDAM is straightforward masking applied to 10% of data (+1-4% gains per Table 3), VTGR uses standard metrics (IoU/IoP/IoG), DAPO borrowed from prior work. Each component is incremental.

Inadequate solution to acknowledged 'fake thinking' problem: Proposed 10% masking is unprincipled, insufficient (failures persist in Figure 15), and lacks theoretical justification. No root-cause analysis of reasoning inconsistency.
Modest empirical improvements: +1.9% on VideoMME, +2.2% on MLVU, +0.9% on LVBench vs. strongest baselines. Gains don't justify system complexity without clearer component attribution.

Experimental fairness issues: Reproduced results marked with * but discrepancies from original papers unexplained. Unclear if improvements from method or evaluation setup. Hyperparameter choices (b₀=0.5, wg=0.5, etc.) appear arbitrary without sensitivity analysis.

Reproducibility and scalability limitations: Reliance on proprietary Gemini 2.5 Pro API for data generation. Self-collected data not promised to be released. Framework narrowly tailored to video cropping; extending to other tools acknowledged as infeasible without major redesign (Appendix J).

Missing critical ablations: No isolation of data quality contribution vs. method. No comparison of synthetic vs. hand-annotated trajectories. No error analysis by task type (single vs. multi-clue reasoning).

strengths: Well-motivated native interleaved tool invocation paradigm addressing a genuine problem in long-form video understanding

Technically sound and practical contributions: TDAM elegantly addresses attention dispersion via visibility constraints (Eq. 1), and VTGR thoughtfully balances exploration-efficiency via IoU-based clue scoring and turn decay

Comprehensive experimental validation across 8 diverse benchmarks (VideoMME, MLVU, Video-Holmes, LVBench, etc.) with consistent improvements; temporal grounding shows substantial gains (mIoU 60.7 vs LongVT 27.2)
Valuable dataset contribution: Seeker-173K provides 173k stratified tool-interaction trajectories with rigorous 4-stage synthesis pipeline addressing data scarcity

Thorough ablation studies (Tables 3-5) validate necessity of each component; turn-limit analysis demonstrates multi-hop reasoning's contribution; 32.9% inference speedup over LOVE-R1 via unified context

Extensive documentation with detailed appendices (A-J) including implementation specifics, additional ablations, qualitative analysis (Figs 11-13), failure cases (Fig 14), and honest limitations discussion
weaknesses: Modest empirical improvements (1-4% on most benchmarks): MLVU +2.2%, Video-Holmes +2.7%, VideoMME +1.9%; gains are consistent but incremental given added complexity, raising questions about practical significance

Identified 'fake thinking' phenomenon (Section 3.2, Appendix I) reveals model fails to coherently leverage retrieved evidence; proposed solution of applying TDAM to only 10% of data is ad-hoc and lacks principled justification for the specific ratio

Data synthesis quality unvalidated: pipeline depends entirely on Gemini 2.5 Pro VLM annotations without reported inter-annotator agreement, error rates, or comparison with human annotations; risk of propagating systematic biases
Limited generalization evidence: primary evaluation on Qwen2.5-VL with only minimal Qwen3-VL-4B testing (Table 7); unclear whether improvements stem from novel methods vs. base model quality
Critical design choices lack justification: dynamic quota values (2048, 4096, 6144) unexplored; Cfree=0.5 arbitrary; TDAM 10% ratio unjustified; hyperparameter sensitivity (b0, wg, λ) not analyzed

High reproducibility barriers: training requires 32 GPUs, relies on proprietary Qwen2.5-VL and Gemini API, no code release mentioned; 32k token context cap and 8-turn limit are hard constraints; 10.2s inference per sample
Evaluation fairness concerns: Table 1 notes reproduced results (*) with unclear baseline conditions; unclear if all methods evaluated under identical token budgets, FPS, and frame limits

Failure modes under-addressed: Figure 14 shows blind exploration can exhaust turns on subtle clues; authors acknowledge but offer no concrete solution, leaving frequency of this failure unknown on real benchmarks
